questions.question: What is the core invariant of a privacy engineering architecture?
options: Every personal-data copy remains linked to an enforceable purpose, owner, retention rule, recipients, and rights workflow
Every service receives the full customer profile after authentication
Encryption removes the need for purpose and retention controls
A compliance dashboard is available to legal reviewers
questions.explanation: Privacy controls must follow every primary, derived, exported, logged, and backed-up copy through its complete lifecycle.

questions.question: A recommendation service requests precise location even though its approved purpose only needs recent product categories. What should the purpose gate do?
options: Allow the field because it may improve a future model
Block or remove the field unless a separately reviewed purpose authorizes it
Store the field indefinitely but hide it from the UI
Replace the purpose ID with a broad analytics label
questions.explanation: Data minimization compares each requested field with the declared purpose before the field enters downstream systems.

questions.question: Why is consent withdrawal more than updating a preference-center row?
options: The system must stop new consent-based processing and revoke downstream grants
The user must create a new account
Withdrawal only changes marketing email templates
Cached consent can remain valid indefinitely
questions.explanation: Withdrawal must propagate to executors, caches, derived uses, and recipients that depend on that consent.

questions.question: Which surface belongs in privacy lineage even when it is not a primary database?
options: Only the customer-facing API
Only encrypted object storage
Derived features, logs, vendor exports, search indexes, and backups
Only records with a person's full legal name
questions.explanation: A copy or derived record can still identify or affect a person and must inherit the purpose and rights contract.

questions.question: A deletion workflow reports success, but four analytics systems have no registered owners. What is the correct architectural conclusion?
options: Deletion is complete because the primary row is gone
The request cannot be proven complete until those locations are discovered and handled
The analytics systems are exempt because they are internal
Increase the backup retention period
questions.explanation: Unknown locations create an evidence gap: the coordinator cannot prove which copies were deleted, restricted, or excepted.

questions.question: How should a system usually describe deletion from inaccessible rotating backups?
options: Claim every byte disappeared immediately
Keep restored data active until the next request
Logically delete active copies, block normal backup access, replay deletion after restore, and document expiry
Disable backups for all personal data
questions.explanation: Backup handling needs an explicit residual-data contract and evidence rather than an impossible immediate-erasure claim.

questions.question: What evidence best supports a defensible subject-request completion record?
options: A screenshot of the request queue
One receipt per owned location tied to the request, policy version, executor, time, action, and exception
A monthly aggregate request count
The current application schema without execution results
questions.explanation: Location-level receipts connect the declared lineage to the operation each executor actually performed.

questions.question: What should happen when a new downstream consumer appears without a reviewed purpose or owner?
options: Allow it until the next annual audit
Assign a random retention period
Stop release or require review before personal data flows to it
Remove the lineage event from monitoring
questions.explanation: Failing closed prevents purpose drift and keeps ownerless copies from silently entering the data estate.
